syllabus.clause: k-way merges with heaps or loser trees in LSM compaction and shuffle reads

at.step: A RocksDB compaction opens twenty sorted files holding four billion keys and writes one sorted, deduplicated output, never holding more than one key per file in memory. A dashboard asks for the ten most expensive orders of four hundred million. Both are a heap. Predict: for the top ten of four hundred million rows, about how many rows actually replace something in the heap, if the rows arrive in random order?

Pebble's mergingIter keeps one heap of child iterators, one per LSM level, table or memtable. The same heap runs forward as a min-heap and backward as a max-heap. Next or Prev pops the current winner, advances its iterator, and "fixes" the heap — pop, advance, sift, read word for word from the source.

RocksDB built the identical design independently: a min/max heap combining data from point iterators. What makes it a database merge and not a generic one is the comparator: ties on the user key are broken by decreasing sequence number, so the newest version of a key surfaces first out of the heap with no special case at all.

A compaction's own input iterator is built the same way: VersionSet::MakeInputIterator opens one iterator per input file across every input level and merges them into a single merging iterator. CompactionIterator then walks that merge and drops every version a newer one has already shadowed, tombstones included.

Predict: twelve streams need to merge, and a tree of losers is a complete binary tree in spirit. Does Velox's TreeOfLosers lay out twelve streams as a tree where every level but the last is completely full, the textbook picture exactly?

Spark's heap shows up through two different APIs, same kernel. UnsafeSorterSpillMerger's priority queue never enqueues an empty spill reader, so a drained reader can never produce a spurious record. ExternalSorter's mergeSort builds a max-heap-only priority queue with the comparator reversed, because dequeuing the "maximum" under a flipped order is dequeuing the minimum key.

Chapter six already measured the cost: at a fan-in of eight, a binary heap spends about 4.35 comparisons per output row; a tree of losers spends exactly log base two of eight, three, every time, a 1.45 times difference. And still, three of the four engines read here reach for the heap, not the loser tree, because it adapts to an uneven fan-in with no separate rebuild step.

syllabus.clause: bounded heaps for ORDER BY … LIMIT

at.step: The same heap, turned upside down. PostgreSQL's make_bounded_heap keeps the largest entry at the root instead of the smallest, temporarily reversing the sort direction, because the root is what a bounded heap needs to discard cheaply. The switch itself fires once the input passes twice the bound, or once work memory fills with enough rows to meet it.

Spark's BoundedPriorityQueue is the same structure for ORDER BY ... LIMIT: capped at the limit, a new row only replaces the current worst kept row when it ranks higher. Utils.takeOrdered runs this per partition, shuffles only those small local winners to one partition, then runs the identical bounded heap once more over the merged result — RDD's own doc comment calls it the opposite of top.

The arithmetic: a full sort costs on the order of n log n comparisons; a bounded heap of size N costs at most n log N, cheaper whenever N is far smaller than n, exactly the ORDER BY ... LIMIT case. And the number of rows that actually replace something in the heap, derived from how a random arrival order ranks each row and checked by simulation before trusting it at scale, is about k times the gap between two harmonic numbers — for ten of four hundred million, about one hundred seventy-five.
